title: Test Synthetic Data for HDT Development
purposes: Other Purpose (This project focuses on technical and methodological validation. The primary goal is to evaluate the functional compatibility of an external synthetic data repository with the Hybrid Digital Twin (HDT) framework within the Verily Workbench. We aim to determine if synthetic cohorts can successfully initialize stateful HDT models while maintaining data integrity. This benchmarking effort will help establish a privacy-preserving pipeline for secondary data analysis and model auditing.)
questions:
The primary scientific question is whether an external synthetic data repository can functionally support the initialization and execution of a Hybrid Digital Twin (HDT) framework within a secure cloud environment. Specifically, does the synthetic data retain the necessary longitudinal depth and clinical coherence to drive stateful digital twin simulations without the use of protected health information (PHI)?

This is important because the scalability of precision medicine depends on developing "environment-agnostic" tools that can move between research platforms. By validating that a synthetic repository can effectively "fuel" an HDT, we can create a blueprint for high-fidelity, privacy-preserving research. This approach allows for rigorous "shadow studies" and model auditing that protect participant privacy while still providing the granular data needed to understand complex disease trajectories and treatment durability in chronic conditions like diabetes.
approaches:
I will employ a technical validation and benchmarking methodology to assess the portability of a local synthetic data repository into the Verily Workbench. The study will utilize two primary datasets: a local WAL SQLite database containing over 3 million rows of longitudinal event data (and its associated 262-column synthetic supplement) and the All of Us Synthetic Dataset v5 for comparative baseline analysis.

Research methods include:

Mapping & Harmonization: Aligning the external synthetic repo schema with the OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) used by the All of Us platform.

Functional Integration: Implementing the Hybrid Digital Twin (HDT) framework within the Workbench environment to test data ingestion and stateful simulation performance.

Integrity Auditing: Using Python-based scripts to verify that the synthetic data maintains clinical coherence when processed through the HDT pipeline.
findings:
I anticipate demonstrating that an external synthetic data repository can successfully initialize a Hybrid Digital Twin (HDT) with high functional fidelity. Specifically, the study expects to prove that synthetic "shadow" cohorts can replicate the longitudinal complexities of real-world patient trajectories without compromising privacy. I expect to confirm that the 262-column synthetic supplement provides sufficient granularity for stateful monitoring within the All of Us Verily Workbench.

These findings will contribute to the field by providing a validated framework for privacy-preserving, "environment-agnostic" biomedical research. By showing that a modular HDT can function seamlessly with synthetic data, this work paves the way for scalable, auditable clinical simulations. This reduces the reliance on sensitive personal health information (PHI) while maintaining the scientific rigor needed to study treatment durability and disease progression.

title: Duplication of racism during the pandemic: mental health among Asian Americans
questions:
This workspace aims to duplicate findings in Chae et al. (2021) study on racism and depressive symptomology among Asian Americans during the COVID19 pandemic. "Experiences of vicarious racism—hearing about racism directed toward one’s racial group or racist acts committed against other racial group members—and vigilance about racial discrimination have been salient during the COVID-19 pandemic."

Chae, D. H., Yip, T., Martz, C. D., Chung, K., Richeson, J. A., Hajat, A., ... & LaVeist, T. A. (2021). Vicarious racism and vigilance during the COVID-19 pandemic: mental health implications among Asian and Black Americans. Public Health Reports, 136(4), 508-517.
approaches:
We improve upon Chae et al. (2021) study by using a longitudinal study of Asian American adults aged ≥18 in the United States recruited from the All of Us Research Program. We will us the COPE survey to examine mental health. Example questions of interest include:

In the past 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by: Little interest or pleasure in doing things
In the past 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by: Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless
In your day-to-day life, how often did this happen to you during the past month? You are threatened or harassed
In your day-to-day life, how often did this happen to you during the past month? People act as if they are afraid of you

Multivariable linear regression models examined levels of depression and anxiety by self- reported vicarious racism and vigilance.
findings: "Mental health problems are a pressing concern during the COVID-19 pandemic. Results from our study suggest that heightened racist sentiment, harassment, and violence against Asian contribute to increased risk of depression and anxiety via vicarious racism and vigilance. Public health efforts during this period should address endemic racism as well as COVID-19."

title: How to Get Started with Registered Tier Data
questions: We recommend that all researchers explore the notebooks in this workspace to learn the basics of All of Us Program Data. What should you expect? This notebook will give you an overview of what data is available in the current Curated Data Repository (CDR). It will also teach you how to retrieve information about Electronic Health Record (EHR), Physical Measurements (PM), and Survey data.
approaches: This Tutorial Workspace contains two Jupyter Notebooks (one written in Python, the other in R). Each notebook is divided into the following sections: 1. Setup: How to set up this notebook, install and import software packages, and select the correct version of the CDR. 2. Data Availability Part 1: How to summarize the number of unique participants with major data types: Physical Measurements, Survey, and EHR; 3. Data Availability Part 2: How to delve a little deeper into data availability within each major data type; 4. Data Organization: An explanation of how data is organized according to our common data model. 5. Example Queries: How to directly query the CDR, using two examples of SQL queries to extract demographic data. 6. Expert Tip: How to access the base version of the CDR, for users that want to do their own cleaning.
findings: By reading and running the notebooks in this Tutorial Workspace, you will understand the following: All of Us data are made available in a Curated Data Repository. Participants may contribute any combination of survey, physical measurement, and electronic health record data. Not all participants contribute all possible data types. Each unique piece of health information is given a unique identifier called a concept_id and organized into specific tables according to our common data model. You can use these concept_ids to query the CDR and pull data on specific health information relevant to your analysis. See our support article Learning the Basics of the All of Us Dataset for more info.
